parole.significato: used to form feminine forms of nouns, especially ones with masculine counterparts in -eur
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -ātrīcem, initially inherited as Old French -eriz; later changed to -eresse under the influence of -esse and superficial analysis as -eur + -esse. Doublet of -atrice, which was borrowed later.

parole.significato: forms the first-person singular present indicative of -ir verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -iō → *-īō, -is → *-īs (sense 1–2); Latin -īvī, and -īvisti (sense 3–4). Inherited from Old French aacier, from Vulgar Latin *adacidare, from Latin acidare, influenced by Old French agu (“needle”) (modern aigu).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assōpīre (“satisfy”), from Latin sōpiō (“to sleep”) (influenced by Old French assevir (“attain”)). Doublet of assoupir.

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French cel, cil, from Vulgar Latin *ecce ille. See also celui, derived from the oblique cases of the same. The inflected forms continue Old French cest, cist, from Vulgar Latin *ecce iste.

parole.significato: chamfer, bevel (obtuse-angled relief or cut at an edge)
parole.testo: From the Old French verb chanfraindre, formed from chant (from Latin canthus) and Old French fraindre.

parole.significato: carnal (relating to the physical and especially sexual appetites)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French charnel, from Old French charnel, inherited from Latin carnālis. Also analysable as a derivative of Old French charn (→ Modern French chair) + -el.
Inherited from Latin convenire. Spelt covenir in Old French, etymologically reconstructed in Middle French to closer match the original Latin spelling.
Inherited from Latin dēnūntiāre (“to announce, foretell”), via Old French denuncier or denuntier (“to denounce”).
From Latin inter- via Old French entre.
From Old French ci (“here”), from Late Latin ecce hīc, with /i-/ added by analogy with Old French iluec (“there, in that place”), from Latin illoc.
After Latin immutābilis (compare immutable) with influence of Old French muable (“subject to change”).

parole.significato: to run again, to race again
parole.testo: From re- + courir, with some senses from Latin recurrere. Found in Old French as recourre, recorre.
From Old French revenchier (from re- + vengier (“to avenge, to take revenge (upon)”, from Latin vindicō)).

Learned reborrowing of Latin re-. Compare re-, r-, the inherited forms. Some verbs in ré- continue Old French res-, a combination of re- + es- (from Latin ex). Compare Romanian răs-, which might have a similar development.

Inherited from Latin secundus (presumably through an earlier Old French form *seon; compare an attested Medieval Latin seonno, seonnum). Cognate with Catalan segó, Old Occitan segon. The meaning derives from the fact that bran results from a second sifting of flour. Doublet of second, a borrowing.

parole.significato: internship, job that a trainee is doing in a workplace until a fixed date
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stagium, itself from Old French estage: ester + -age (whence modern French étage).
